Module Seven Activity¶

For the module seven activity, you will identify relevant data and write Python code to generate visualizations and interpret insights from the provided data set. Professionals in data-driven fields must not only interpret data but also gather, analyze, and present it in meaningful and actionable ways. This activity allows you to practice these essential skills by working through the complete exploratory data analysis (EDA) process.

Note: there are two parts to this assignment. Part One is the coding activity. Part Two is the written report.

Once your code is complete, you will download this notebook as an HTML file by clicking File, then Download As, then HTML (.html) from the Jupyter menu bar. Validate that your code, output, and all visualizations (rendered as images using the display() function) are visible in the html file before submission.

Missing Blocks: Ensure that you have clicked Run for all blocks before downloading as an HTML file or the block may be missing from your submission. Images must be called using the display() function, for example: display(Image(filename="output/{image_name}.png"))

# strip whitespace, and remove commas
def clean_for_int(x):
    return x.strip().replace(',', '')
    
# strip whitespace, remove the $, and remove commas
def clean_for_float(x):
    return x.strip().replace('$', '').replace(',', '')

# convert whole number columns to ints
to_ints = ["Passenger Miles FY", "Unlinked Passenger Trips FY"]
for column in to_ints:
    neighborhood_data[column] = neighborhood_data[column].apply(clean_for_int)
    neighborhood_data[column] = neighborhood_data[column].astype(int)


# convert dollar columns to floats
to_floats = ["Fares FY", "Operating Expenses FY", "Avg Cost Per Trip FY", "Avg Fares Per Trip FY"]
for column in to_floats:
    neighborhood_data[column] = neighborhood_data[column].apply(clean_for_float)
    neighborhood_data[column] = neighborhood_data[column].astype(float)

# display the same row after cleaning

Generate, Save, and Output Visualizations¶

These are simple example frameworks that you may use, but you may, and are encouraged to develop your own visualizations that you will then explain how the selected visualizations support your conclusions in the part two report.
In accordance with the scenario, three neighborhoods for evaluation are: King County, City of Longview, and Spokane Transit Authority which have been listed in the neighborhoods variable above.

Visualization 1: Line chart of ridership trends over years¶

This is an example visualization you can generate. You may implement a chart and assessment of your choosing in lieu of this placeholder.

At a minimum include the following actions:¶

  • Add title and axis labels
  • Save the plot to a png file in the 'output' folder
  • Use the display() function to render the generated png image in the html output
  • Comments explaining each step of your analysis
In [12]:
# To Do: Create a visualization that will support your conclusions for part two

# VISUALIZATION 1
# Compare fare revenue and operating expenses for each of the 3 neighborhoods/agencies.

# aggregate the data by Agency
aggregated = df.groupby("Agency")[["Operating Expenses FY", "Fares FY"]].sum().reset_index()

# sort agencies by Operating Expenses descending (most expensive first)
aggregated = aggregated.sort_values(by="Operating Expenses FY", ascending=False)

# melt for a Seaborn grouped bar chart
melted = aggregated.melt(id_vars="Agency", value_vars=["Fares FY", "Operating Expenses FY"],
                         var_name="Financial Metric", value_name="USD")

# legend labels
melted["Financial Metric"] = melted["Financial Metric"].replace({
    "Fares FY": "Fare Revenue",
    "Operating Expenses FY": "Operating Expenses"
})

# set style and plot
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.barplot(data=melted, x="Agency", y="USD", hue="Financial Metric", ax=ax, palette="Set2")

# set the y-axis to be logarithmic since King County dwarfs the other two
plt.yscale('log')
# format the y-axis numbers with commas for clean readability
ax.get_yaxis().set_major_formatter(ticker.FuncFormatter(lambda x, p: f"${int(x):,}"))

# chart labels
ax.set_title("Operating Expenses vs. Fare Revenue by Agency (FY2023)", fontsize=14, pad=15)
ax.set_xlabel("Transit Agency", fontsize=12)
ax.set_ylabel("USD ($)", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(title="Metric")

# also want to show how much of the operating expenses are recovered by the fare revenue
# calculate the percentages
aggregated["percent"] = (aggregated['Fares FY'] / aggregated['Operating Expenses FY']) * 100
# round to 2 decimal places for presentation
aggregated["percent"] = aggregated["percent"].round(2)

# create overlay labels
percents = dict(zip(aggregated['Agency'], aggregated['percent']))
ax.text(0, 900000000, f"{percents['King County']}% Recovery", ha='center', va='bottom', color='black')
ax.text(1, 120000000, f"{percents['Spokane Transit Authority']}% Recovery", ha='center', va='bottom', color='black')
ax.text(2, 6000000, f"{percents['City of Longview']}% Recovery", ha='center', va='bottom', color='black')

# save and display!
plt.tight_layout()
image_name = "expenses_vs_revenue_by_agency_FY2023"
plt.savefig(f"output/{image_name}.png", dpi=300)
plt.close()
display(Image(filename=f"output/{image_name}.png"))

# To Do: Create a visualization that will support your conclusions for part two

# VISUALIZATION 2: bar chart for total ridership by agency

# group by Agency and '3 Mode' (bus, rail, or ferry) to sum up the ridership
ridership_grouped = df.groupby(['Agency', '3 Mode'])['Unlinked Passenger Trips FY'].sum().reset_index()

# sort by ridership descending
ridership_grouped = ridership_grouped.sort_values(by='Unlinked Passenger Trips FY', ascending=False)

# plot layout
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 6))

# create the grouped bar chart, x-axis the agency and a bar for each transit type
sns.barplot(
    data=ridership_grouped, 
    x='Agency', 
    y='Unlinked Passenger Trips FY', 
    hue='3 Mode', 
    ax=ax, 
    palette='Set2'
)

# log scale so King County doesn't dwarf the other two
ax.set_yscale('log')

# format y-axis as full numbers not scientific notation
ax.get_yaxis().set_major_formatter(ticker.FuncFormatter(lambda x, p: f"{int(x):,}"))

# chart labels
ax.set_title("Ridership by Type and Agency (FY2023)", fontsize=14, pad=15)
ax.set_xlabel("Transit Agency", fontsize=12)
ax.set_ylabel("Unlinked Passenger Trips", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(title="Transit Type (3 Mode)", loc='upper right')

# save and display!
plt.tight_layout()
image_name = "ridership_breakdown_FY2023"
plt.savefig(f"output/{image_name}.png", dpi=300)
plt.close()
display(Image(filename=f"output/{image_name}.png"))

# To Do: Create a visualization that will support your conclusions for part two

# VISUALIZATION 3: bubble chart for trip length vs cost and number of trips by agency
# NOTE: creating one for all 17 values and one for just FY23 to show change

# plot layout
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))

# bubble chart, total trips -> bubble size
sns.scatterplot(
    data=neighborhood_data,
    x='Avg Trip Length FY',
    y='Avg Cost Per Trip FY',
    hue='Agency',
    size='Unlinked Passenger Trips FY',
    sizes=(40, 400),  # sets the min and max bubble sizes
    alpha=0.75, # transparency for overlapping bubbles
    palette='muted',
    ax=ax
)

# format y-axis for dollar amounts
ax.get_yaxis().set_major_formatter(ticker.FuncFormatter(lambda x, p: f"${int(x)}"))
# format x-axis for miles
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(ticker.FuncFormatter(lambda x, p: f"{int(x)} mi"))

# chart labels
ax.set_title("Transit Efficiency: Trip Length vs. Cost Per Trip", fontsize=14, pad=20)
ax.text(0.5, 1.03, "Including Inactive Reporting Units", fontsize=10, color='#555555', style='italic', ha='center', va='center', transform=ax.transAxes)
ax.set_xlabel("Average Trip Length (Miles)", fontsize=12)
ax.set_ylabel("Average Cost Per Trip (USD)", fontsize=12)

# make sure legend doesn't overlap plot
ax.legend(bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 1), loc='upper left', title="Agency / Scale", labelspacing=1)

# add a callout for the Longview outlier, which is the focal point of this chart
ax.annotate(
    "Critical Outlier:\n  Longview Vanpool\n  56 miles | $606.33 per trip\n  (18 total trips)",
    xy=(56, 606.33), 
    xytext=(30, 400),  
    textcoords='data',
    fontsize=9,
    color='black',
    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.5", fc="white", ec="red", lw=1.5, alpha=0.9),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.1", color="red", lw=2)
)

# save and display!
plt.tight_layout()
image_name = "trip_length_vs_cost"
plt.savefig(f"output/{image_name}.png", dpi=300)
plt.close()
display(Image(filename=f"output/{image_name}.png"))
